To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Junk‐food (JFD) exposure during development reduced weight gain, but increased motivation for food cues in two strains of rat.
junk‐food consumption during development results in large individual differences (gainers and nongainers) in weight gain and behavior (‘want’ and ‘like’).
Junk‐food exposure during early development has long‐lasting effects on motivation and reward‐related behavior in rats.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of a junk-food (jF) diet during early development on motivation, hedonic ‘likin’, weight gain and anxiety-like behavior.
the impact of a junk‐food (Jf) diet on motivation and reward systems during development.
the effects of junk-food consumption in the developing brain.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
junk‐food consumption during development can result in differential effects on ‘liking’ (sucrose) and ‘wanting’, which are dependent on strain, gender, and the degree of weight gain.
junk‐food diets during development may have long‐lasting effects on the development of motivation and reward systems that are not detected by weight gain.

junk‐food consumption during development can have a profound impact on the development of brain reward and motivational systems that may contribute to the development of eating disorders and obesity.
the impact of junk‐food consumption on brain reward systems is dependent on the sex of the rat, and the genetic background.
